reason: The court held that section 175(1) permits an unlisted witness only where special circumstances make it advisable in the interests of justice.
The court construed section 523 and held that the pleadings disclosed a conflict of claims requiring the executor's claim to prevail over the widow's.
The substitution rule is supported, but the cited statute identifier is Rent Act section 36 rather than Finance Act section 71.
The court expressly left open whether a testate heir had priority over specified heirs, and the statute identifier is also wrong.
The passage is a fact finding that separation, division, and adverse possession were proved, not a rule that those matters are evidence under section 10.
The statement is only a background statutory premise and omits the operative jurisdictional point about inquiries into post-enrolment professional conduct.
The court applied section 42(2) and held that an Attorney-at-Law guilty of deceit or malpractice may be suspended or removed.
The central holding was that the Supreme Court retained jurisdiction to inquire into each rule concerning conduct qua Attorney-at-Law despite prior removal.
The parenthetical records that Wadugodapitiya J. dissented, not that the court's decision was based on the dissent.
The proposition is part of the holding, but it omits material qualifications about severance, rebuttal of registration, and binna readmission.
The statement drops the material words that the marriage continues as binna or diga only until dissolved and as the case may be.
The misconduct finding is real, but the extracted statement is too general and omits the specific retainer, fee, conflict, and failure-to-return-money circumstances.
The statement says no holding is available although the judgment and headnote contain actual professional-misconduct holdings.
The court held that a state-authorised deed of dedication alone did not make the temple Sanghika property without dedication according to Vinaya.
The court dealt with a particular non-party with no apparent right in execution proceedings, not a general rule that any non-party has no right to possession.
The burden rule is supported, but it omits the material condition that the plaintiff's legal title was admitted or proved in a vindicatory claim.
The court held that section 25(b) does not require a recognised agent's general power of attorney to be filed when the plaint is filed.
The statement is an incomplete fragment and therefore cannot state the court's rule.
The court held that the first proviso to section 175(1) gives the trial judge discretion to allow an unlisted witness where special circumstances justify it.
The court upheld refusal only because no special circumstances or explanation were shown, which the extracted statement omits.
The statement is a vague fragment and the cited Civil Procedure Code section was only analogical, not the provision construed for the admiralty holding.
The counterclaim rule is the holding, but the cited statute identifier points to CPC section 654 rather than the Admiralty Jurisdiction Act provision construed.
The revision point is supported, but the statement omits the exceptional facts of collusion, refusal of intervention, and total want of title investigation.
The statement omits that the order was a refusal under Partition Law section 48(4)(a)(iv) and was treated as an order requiring leave under section 754(2).
The statement is too vague to express any rule decided by the court.
